Tasks 3.8 + 3.10 · updated 2026-08-05

Thirty years, promoted in two forms

Thirty-one rings, one per year since Easter 1997, weighted by what the band actually did. Round C drew it on 2026-07-31 and it has sat unpromoted since. Preparing it for a shirt found three things wrong with a drawing everyone admired — including that the one ring meaning not yet was telling a lie in one colour. Task 3.10 then promoted the same ledger as the pulse used across the system.

This report records what one round explored and what it concluded. Where a direction was chosen, that is Marcus’s call, not the band’s — taken so the next stage wasn’t blocked. The band has not reviewed any of it, and it can still change.

Start with the plain-language overview if you haven’t already.

1

What this is, and what it is not

Thirty-one concentric rings, one for every year from Easter 1997 to 2027. Each ring’s weight comes from how much the band actually did that year — gigs, releases, recordings — taken from the verified history in band-facts.md. Count the rings and the biography audits.

The drawing itself is not new. It came out of design round C on 2026-07-31, where it was never in contention as a logo — it falls apart at small sizes — and was set aside as the most beautiful object round C produced, beautiful because it is true. It has been sitting in its round folder since, unpromoted, waiting for a surface that needed it.

This round is the promotion, and it was asked for by name. Marcus, after the large-format session shipped the skull illustration and the shard backgrounds: “the large format session made everything else, but the circle element… I would like to generate the assets for it too. As it is an element that can be used on a variety of stuff. Especially clothing that the shards was scoped out of.”

That last sentence turned out to be the whole argument — see §2 — and preparing the drawing for real use found three things wrong with it that admiring it had not.

These are finished files — with three hard limits

Unlike most of the pages in this set, the pictures here are the deliverable, not concepts. Six colourways are in assets/large-format/rings/ as scalable vector masters. But:

1. This is not a logo and never goes where the logo goes. It is a surface — a poster, a shirt back, a label, a website hero. The mark lives in assets/logos/.

2. Never use it small. Not a preference; measured. See §4.

3. Nothing here has been printed. The print files are made at exact physical size and are ready to hand to a printer. A screen is not a proof, and this project has already been caught out once by assuming otherwise.

2

Why the rings and not the shards — a licence, not a preference

The brand has two large-format surfaces: these rings and the gold shard fields built last session. The documents have always treated them as a matched pair, two options for the same job. For anything sold, they are not a pair at all, and this is the finding that justified doing the work now rather than at website time.

The shard fields are AI-generated images. That was the right call for a background and it is recorded in full in the large-format report. But the licence covering generated images, read on 2026-08-03, says two things that matter here:

  • on merchandise sold to more than one buyer, a generated resource “must be a secondary element of the design — not the main visual focus”;
  • and the separate merchandise licence that would lift that restriction “covers non-AI Premium files only. AI-generated resources are excluded.”

On a shirt back, the artwork is the main visual focus. So the shard fields cannot be the front-and-centre image on merch — they can sit behind something else, or not be used.

The rings have no generated content in them at all. The geometry is arithmetic and the data is the band’s own history. Nothing about them is licensed from anybody, which also matters if the band ever registers a trademark.

So, plainly

Of the brand’s two large-format surfaces, only the rings can be the main event on something you sell. Marcus reached that conclusion from the shape of the previous session; the licence is the reason it is correct.

3

The 2027 ring was described as hollow. It was not.

The brand documents describe the outermost ring as “hollow, amber, and the surface’s one warm element” — the one open question drawn as the one warm thing. The drawing does not match that description. Every ring in round C’s file, 2027 included, is a solid band. 2027 is just slightly thicker than its neighbours, and amber.

In colour that reads perfectly, because the amber carries the meaning, and nobody noticed. Take the colour away — which is exactly what a single-screen shirt does — and the ring stops meaning anything. Here is why, measured:

RingThickness, in bands
A silent year0.100
1 event0.290← round C’s 2027 sits here
Round C’s 2027 ring0.300a solid band, not a void
2 events0.352
3 events0.400
4 events0.440
17 events0.759
23 events0.860
2027 as it now ships0.440two lines with a gap — no count can be a hole

Round C’s 2027 ring is within one hundredth of a band of a one-event year. So on a one-colour shirt, the ring whose entire job is to say this has not happened yet instead says a couple of things happened in 2027 that nobody wrote down. In a drawing whose whole claim is that it is true, that is not a styling wrinkle. It is a false statement, and it was already sitting in the round folder in a file called rings-mono.svg, ready for the exact use this round was asked for.

It now ships as a real hole: two fine lines with a gap between them. No amount of activity can look like a gap, in any colour or none.

This is a return to the system, not a new idea

The same round, from the same data, also drew this history as a horizontal strip — the pulse that sits under the wordmark on posters. In that strip, 2027 has always been drawn as a genuine hollow tick. So the rings were the version that had drifted away from the rule, not the version setting it.

4

How big it has to be — and the answer is set by the empty years

The rule has always been large format only, on good evidence: shrink this drawing and the rings interfere with each other into a moiré smear. But that evidence was all about screens, and it gave no answer at all to the question a printer asks: how many millimetres wide? The skull illustration has that number, measured on paper. The rings did not.

The limit turns out to come from an unexpected place. The thinnest line in the drawing is not a busy year — it is a silent one, and twenty-one of the thirty-one years are silent. So how large this can be printed is decided by the years when nothing happened, which is either an irony or precisely the point.

A silent ring is 0.131% of the artwork’s width. In practice:

SurfaceWidth Thinnest lineOn fabric?
Shirt back print, wide320 mm0.418 mmoffered
A3 poster, full width297 mm0.388 mmoffered
Shirt back print, typical280 mm0.366 mmoffered
Shirt front print250 mm0.327 mmoffered
Vinyl centre label120 mm0.157 mmpaper only
Vinyl label, inner100 mm0.131 mmpaper only
Sticker / pick60 mm0.078 mmno

Even across a wide shirt back the line is under half a millimetre. Whether that survives depends on the printing method, the mesh, the ink and the cloth — and this report does not invent a threshold for that, the same position the brand takes on print colour. The numbers above are what to hand a printer. What is decided: nothing below 250 mm is offered for fabric, and small items like stickers and guitar picks are out.

If a printer says it is too fine — Marcus’s call

The fix would be to make all twenty-one silent rings slightly thicker together. That keeps the ring count exactly right, so the drawing stays true; it only flattens the contrast between the busy years and the quiet ones. That is a change to how the artwork looks, so it is not a decision this round took on its own.

On screen, the real floor is 800 pixels — not 96

The existing rule quotes 96 px as where the drawing breaks. That is where the moiré starts. The more useful number is where every ring still carries a full pixel of ink, and that is 765 px — 804 px for a clear pixel between the two heaviest neighbours.

Which means round C’s own celebrated picture of this drawing is below its own floor. It renders at 620 px, where a silent ring is 0.81 of a pixel — so it comes out as grey rather than ink. The most admired object in round C has twenty-one faded rings, and nobody had measured it. Nothing here ships below 800 px.

5

“The drawing changes only if the history changes” — now enforced

The strongest rule attached to this artwork is that nobody adjusts a ring by eye. If the band’s history is corrected, the drawing is rebuilt from the corrected history — that is what makes it worth anything. Nothing was checking.

Round C kept the year-by-year figures typed into its own build script, with the reasons in code comments. So the artwork and the verified history in band-facts.md were two separate copies of the same thing, and nothing ever compared them. band-facts.md was then edited three times on 2026-08-03 — after the drawing was made.

The numbers happened to still be right. That is luck, not a process — and it is what started this round, because the drawing was asserting that 2026 was silent on the strength of a copy nobody had reconciled.

What it does now

The ledger lives in one place, and every one of its twenty entries carries the exact sentence from band-facts.md that proves it. A check reads the history file and refuses to build if any of those sentences has been rewritten or removed. It reports 20 / 20 evidenced.

Its own limit, stated because it matters: this proves nothing the drawing rests on has been changed. It cannot prove the ledger is complete — no script can spot a gig that ought to be in the file and is not. So the check also fingerprints the history file and says REVIEW when it moves, which dates a human’s reading rather than pretending to replace it.

2026 is drawn silent, and it is the ring that moves first

band-facts.md records that the band went to five and reassembled in August 2026, with the first five-piece rehearsal on Friday 7 August. Marcus’s call, 2026-08-03: silent. The ledger counts gigs, releases, recordings and broadcasts; a lineup change is none of those, and the rehearsal is four days after this was built. Counting it would state something that has not happened, which is the exact thing 2027’s hollow ring exists to avoid.

So the drawing did not move at all — the ledger reproduces round C’s figures exactly, and the build checks that rather than claiming it. That matters more than tidiness: the same history feeds the pulse strip, which is used on gate 5’s poster and header and across the whole social media set. A changed ledger would have quietly invalidated finished files in three other folders. It did not.

After the rehearsal, one line changes and everything rebuilds. That is the rule working rather than being quoted.

Three readings are contested, and none is settled here

Parts of this band’s own history are still unresolved, and the drawing has to take a position to exist at all. Each position is recorded with what it would change, and each is tied to the wording in band-facts.md that records the doubt — so if a question settles, the check flags it instead of silently keeping the old answer.

One contradiction surfaced in the history file itself

Not this round’s to fix, but it should not sit unrecorded: band-facts.md states “Summer 1998 — first EP, Unbalanced” in its timeline, while its own detailed analysis of the same question concludes “1999 is the better bet”. The file disagrees with itself. The ledger follows the analysis.

6

Checks, and two that were wrong about a correct file

Every shipped file is opened again after it is written and measured against the brand’s colour rules — no red, no Steel used as line work, the warm accent matching its background and staying under 2% of the surface, and the one-colour files containing no colour at all. All sixteen checks pass.

The vector and the picture are checked against each other

A printer works from the scalable vector file; everything else looks at the picture. Those come out of two separate pieces of code, which is exactly the arrangement where two things quietly stop being the same drawing. So each vector master is loaded back in, drawn by an independent renderer, and compared against the picture pixel by pixel: 0.000% of pixels disagree.

An amber edge counts as brass, and the fix broke the other check

Two of the checks failed on files that are correct, and both are worth recording because the next person will hit them.

The brand uses amber on dark backgrounds and a darker brass on light ones, and a check makes sure a surface does not mix them up. On this drawing it reported 6 552 violations on a clean file. The reason: brass is a darker amber, so every softened edge of every amber ring passes through brass on its way down to the background. The skull plates never hit this, because nothing warm touches them. A drawing made of thirty-one thin circles is almost entirely edge. Fixed by looking for a wrong-coloured shape rather than a wrong-coloured pixel.

That fix then broke the neighbouring check, which counts how many separate warm things are on a surface: it reported 276 where there are 2, because the same technique shatters a circle two and a half pixels thick. Two checks, two methods, one reason each. The tempting single setting that satisfies both does not exist.

Why the answer is two, not one

The brand allows one warm element per surface. The hollow 2027 ring is one ring drawn as two lines — the way a letter O is one letter with two edges. The check expects exactly 2 rather than being relaxed, so that a genuine third warm thing still fails.

7

On a shirt — decided

Settled by Marcus, 2026-08-03

The shirt is the rings with the name under them — the gold 2027 ring, APEZONE, then HELSINKI · 1997–2027. “The one with the text and the circle is awesome!”

It is a two-colour print, and both colourways are kept: gold-plus-grey where two screens are available, grey alone where they are not. Print-ready files, separated by screen, are in assets/large-format/rings/garment/.

This overrules the front-and-back split recommended further down this section, which is left standing rather than quietly deleted — the reasoning behind it is still the reasoning, it just did not win.

Marcus, on first seeing the colourways: “I would use the one with the golden ring on black/dark shirt.” That reads better than the alternative at print size — but it quietly changes the job, in three ways worth knowing before anything is quoted.

1. It is not the file that looks like it. The dark version in the set carries a solid near-black background, which is correct on paper and wrong on cloth — printing it means laying a near-black square onto a near-black shirt. On a garment the garment is the background, so the file has nothing behind the rings.

2. It is a two-colour print — two screens, not one. Pale grey for the rings, gold for 2027. Both separations are in assets/large-format/rings/garment/, because a printer needs them apart as well as together.

3. The registration is unusually easy, and that is measured. The gold ring is the outermost one and touches nothing: there is 2.67 mm of bare shirt between it and the nearest grey ring at 280 mm. The two screens share no edge anywhere, so nothing has to line up precisely and no overlap needs allowing for.

And the one-screen version is still honest — which is the point of §3

If two screens is not worth it, a single grey screen still works, because 2027 is now a hole rather than a gold band. It still says not yet in one colour. Before this round it would have said something happened in 2027. Compared at print size the gold reads considerably better, so the pick is also the better picture — but the cheap option is no longer a lie.

The mockups — and what is real in them

The shirt is AI-generated. The artwork is not. Asked to put “the logo on a t-shirt”, an image generator invents a ring pattern that looks plausible — which would be a made-up mark presented as this band's mark, and it would mean nothing, because the whole value of this drawing is that the number of rings is the real history. So the blank garment is generated and the rings are the actual shipped file, composited on afterwards, shaded by the shirt's own folds so it sits in the cloth.

The garments were generated with nobody in them — no model, no hands. The rules for this brand forbid generated photographs of people, and a mockup gains nothing by testing that line.

These mockups cannot be used to sell anything

The generated shirt is most of the picture, and §2's licence restriction applies to it: a generated image cannot be the main visual focus of merchandise. So the mockups are for deciding what to make, not for a shop listing or an advert.

The irony is worth stating plainly: the rings are the element we can put on a shirt precisely because nothing in them is generated — and a picture of them on a shirt is unusable commercially because the shirt is. A real product photo needs a real printed garment.

The size is honest too: the print is placed at a measured 62% of the garment's chest width. The millimetre figure on each sheet is marked assumed, because nothing in a generated photograph tells you how big the shirt really is.

What had to be rebuilt once it was chosen

The approved image was not a file. It existed only inside the mockup script, as a composite of pictures: the wordmark rasterised and the years set as live type. That is fine for showing someone, and useless for a printer, who needs outlines.

So it was rebuilt as one vector file — the rings from the same geometry as everything else, the wordmark’s own curves moved but never redrawn, and the years converted to outlines, so no font is needed downstream and nothing can be substituted for Barlow by accident. The separations check out: 37 shapes on the grey screen, 1 on the gold, 38 together.

One number to check before ordering

The files are 280 mm wide and about 346 mm tall — but the visible circle inside that is only about 256 mm, because the name and years share the width. The thinnest line is unchanged at 0.366 mm. If the circle itself should be 280 mm, the whole thing needs to be about 307 mm wide.

8

The same record, drawn as a pulse

The rings are the large-format form. The pulse is the same thirty-one years drawn as a strip: one station per year, height by documented activity, and a hollow amber 2027 tick for not yet. It appears on more surfaces than the rings do — posters, social headers, end cards and the site.

Until task 3.10 it was still being read directly from round C, and round C’s build carried a second hardcoded copy of the ledger. The rings had gained a facts gate; the pulse used everywhere else had not. Both now read rings-build/activity.py, and check_activity.py checks the built pulse manifest against the same 31 stations and the same band-facts.md digest.

The drawing was not redesigned. Every bar and the baseline keep round C’s coordinates, asserted before the files are written. The old SVG did carry 37% dead height below the baseline; the promoted master’s viewBox is the exact ink box, so consumers no longer crop it independently.

Now a real asset

Four SVG colourways and two 2400-pixel placement files live in assets/large-format/pulse/. The pulse is layout furniture, not a logo and not a surface on its own.

9

Method, and what is still open

Method

  • Zero images generated for the artwork. The geometry is arithmetic; the data is the band’s own documented record. No AI-generated content is in any shipped file in assets/.
  • Four generated blank garments, 400 credits, for the mockups in §7 only — wordless, subjectless, nobody in frame. Those live in the working folder, not in assets/, and each sheet says on its face that the garment is generated.
  • The geometry is round C’s, unchanged and verified as such — 31 radii and 30 thicknesses checked against round C’s own formulas, plus its year-by-year figures. Only the renderer changed, and only because concentric circles can be drawn by direct calculation where the old route would need about 6 GB of memory for an A3 sheet. The one intentional difference is the 2027 ring, §3.
  • Six colourways, each a scalable vector master plus a 3000 px picture, and four print files at exact physical size. The vectors are outlined shapes rather than stroked lines, so nothing downstream has to convert them — and nobody converts them wrongly.

What this round did not do

  • Nothing has been printed, and nothing is ordered. The print files exist at true physical size for exactly that purpose. A screen render is not a proof.
  • Whether the silent rings need thickening for fabric is open — a printer’s answer first, then Marcus’s. §4.
  • The caption’s final wording is not settled here. The sentence one ring per year since Easter 1997 has to appear once somewhere findable, or the whole encoding is invisible and this reads as decoration. It is in the folder’s README and deliberately not burned into the artwork, because the wording belongs to the website task.
  • No posters or merch layouts ship from here. One example surface exists as evidence; the real layouts belong to the merch and website tasks.
  • The 2026 ring — one line, after 7 August.
  • The band has not seen this yet.
